p.src: Now Sima Yi, routed in a charge by Zhang Yi and Liao Hua, fled toward a dense forest with only his horse and spear. Zhang Yi halted the rear troops while Liao Hua led the pursuit. Just as Liao Hua was about to catch him, Sima Yi panicked and circled around a tree. Liao Hua slashed at him, but his blade struck the tree squarely. By the time he pulled out his blade, Sima Yi had already escaped from the forest. Liao Hua raced out after him but could not tell where he had gone; he saw only a golden helmet lying east of the forest. Liao Hua picked up the helmet, hung it from his horse, and rode straight east in pursuit. In fact, Sima Yi had cast his golden helmet east of the forest and then fled west instead. After pursuing him for some distance without finding a trace, Liao Hua rode out of the valley, met Jiang Wei, and returned with him to camp to see Kongming. Zhang Ni had already driven the wooden oxen and gliding horses back to camp. When the stores had been handed over, the captured grain amounted to more than ten thousand shi. Liao Hua presented the golden helmet and was credited with the foremost merit. Wei Yan was displeased and voiced his resentment, but Kongming pretended not to notice.

p.src: Meanwhile, Sima Yi escaped back to camp, deeply vexed. Suddenly an imperial envoy arrived bearing an edict: Eastern Wu had invaded along three routes, the court was deliberating whom to send against it, and Sima Yi and his commanders were ordered to hold fast and not give battle. Having received the command, Sima Yi deepened his moats, raised his ramparts, and held his position without emerging.

p.src: When Cao Rui heard that Sun Quan was advancing in three divisions, he likewise dispatched three forces to meet him: Liu Shao was ordered to relieve Jiangxia, Tian Yu to relieve Xiangyang, while Cao Rui himself led the main army with Man Chong to relieve Hefei. Man Chong first led a force to the mouth of Lake Chao, where he saw countless warships off the eastern shore, their banners drawn up in perfect order. Man Chong entered the imperial camp and petitioned the ruler of Wei: “The men of Wu will surely take our distant arrival lightly and cannot yet have made preparations. Tonight we can take advantage of their unpreparedness and raid their naval camp; complete victory will surely be ours.” The ruler of Wei said, “Your words accord perfectly with my own intention.” He immediately ordered the valiant general Zhang Qiu to lead five thousand soldiers, each equipped with incendiary materials, and attack from the lake mouth; Man Chong was to lead another five thousand and attack from the eastern shore. That night, during the second watch, Zhang Qiu and Man Chong each led their troops stealthily toward the lake mouth. As they neared the naval camp, both forces raised a great cry and charged in. The Wu troops fell into confusion and fled without fighting. The Wei forces set fires on every side, destroying countless warships, provisions, and implements. Zhuge Jin led the defeated troops in flight to Miankou. The Wei troops returned in great triumph.

p.src: The next day, scouts reported the news to Lu Xun. Lu Xun gathered his commanders and said, “I shall submit a memorial to our sovereign, requesting that he lift the siege of Xincheng and cut off the Wei army’s road of retreat with his troops. I shall lead my forces against their front; unable to withstand us at both head and tail, they can be broken in a single charge.” All approved his proposal. Lu Xun at once composed a memorial and sent a junior officer to carry it secretly to Xincheng. The officer accepted the order and carried the memorial as far as the ferry, where unexpectedly he was seized by Wei troops lying in ambush along the road and taken to their camp before Cao Rui, ruler of Wei. Cao Rui found Lu Xun’s memorial on him and, after reading it, sighed, “Lu Xun of Eastern Wu is truly a brilliant strategist!” He ordered the Wu soldier placed under guard, then commanded Liu Shao to watch carefully for Sun Quan’s following forces.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Zhuge Jin’s crushing defeat, the summer heat caused much sickness among his men and horses. He therefore wrote a letter and had it relayed to Lu Xun, proposing that they withdraw and return home. After reading it, Lu Xun told the messenger, “Convey my respects to the general and tell him that I have a plan of my own.” The messenger returned and reported to Zhuge Jin. Zhuge Jin asked, “What is General Lu doing?” The messenger replied, “I saw only that General Lu was urging the men to plant beans outside the camp, while he and the other commanders amused themselves with archery at the camp gate.” Greatly alarmed, Zhuge Jin went in person to Lu Xun’s camp and met with him. He asked, “Now that Cao Rui has come in person and his army is so powerful, how does the commander-in-chief intend to withstand him?” Lu Xun said, “Earlier I sent a man to present a memorial to our sovereign, but unexpectedly it fell into enemy hands. Now that the plan has been exposed, the enemy will surely be prepared. There is no profit in fighting; we had better withdraw for now. I have already sent a messenger with a memorial asking our sovereign to withdraw his forces gradually.” Zhuge Jin said, “Since that is the commander-in-chief’s intention, we should retreat at once. Why delay any longer?” Lu Xun replied, “If our army is to withdraw, it must move slowly. If we retreat now, the Wei troops will surely pursue us in the flush of their advantage; that is the road to defeat. You should first oversee the ships and feign an intention to resist the enemy. I shall advance all my men and horses toward Xiangyang to deceive them; afterward we shall gradually withdraw to Jiangdong, and the Wei troops will naturally not dare approach us.” Zhuge Jin followed his plan. Lu Xun took his leave and returned to his own camp, while Zhuge Jin put the ships in order and prepared to depart. Lu Xun marshaled his ranks, made a great show of force, and advanced toward Xiangyang.

p.src: Wei spies had already informed their ruler that the Wu army was on the move and precautions were necessary. On hearing this, all the Wei commanders asked to give battle. The ruler of Wei had long known Lu Xun’s ability and warned his commanders, “Lu Xun is resourceful. This may well be a scheme to lure us out; we must not move rashly.” The commanders therefore desisted. Several days later, a scout came and reported, “All three armies of Eastern Wu have withdrawn.” The ruler of Wei did not believe it and sent more men to investigate; they returned and reported that the Wu forces had indeed all withdrawn. The ruler of Wei sighed, “Lu Xun’s conduct of war is no whit inferior to Sun Wu’s. The southeast cannot yet be pacified.” He therefore ordered his commanders to guard the strategic passes, while he led the main army to garrison Hefei and await developments.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming, planning a prolonged stay at Qishan, ordered the Shu soldiers to cultivate the fields together with the people of Wei: for every one part soldiers there were two parts civilians. The troops committed no offenses, and the Wei people all lived and worked in peace. Sima Shi went to his father and said, “The Shu troops have plundered so much of our grain, and now they are mixing with our people and establishing military farms along the Wei River as a long-term plan. If this continues, they will truly become a grave menace to the state. Father, why not appoint a day for a decisive battle with Kongming and settle which side is stronger?” Sima Yi replied, “I have received an imperial command to hold fast and may not move rashly.” While they were still discussing the matter, a sudden report came that Wei Yan was approaching to challenge them, wearing the golden helmet their commander-in-chief had lost the other day. The commanders were furious and all wished to go out and fight. Sima Yi laughed and said, “The Sage said, ‘Impatience in small matters ruins great designs.’ Our best course is simply to hold fast.” The commanders obeyed and did not emerge. Wei Yan hurled abuse at them for a long time before returning.

p.src: Seeing that Sima Yi refused to give battle, Kongming secretly ordered Ma Dai to construct wooden palisades, dig deep trenches within the camp, and amass dry firewood and other combustibles. On the surrounding hills, he had brushwood piled into sham huts, with mines planted both inside and outside them. When all was ready, Kongming whispered his instructions: “Block the rear exit of Gourd Valley and conceal troops within the valley. If Sima Yi pursues you there, let him enter the valley, then ignite the mines and dry firewood all at once.” He also ordered the soldiers to display a seven-star signal banner at the valley mouth by day and set seven bright lamps upon the hill by night as secret signals. Ma Dai received the plan and led his troops away. Kongming then summoned Wei Yan and instructed him: “Take five hundred men to challenge the Wei camp, and make certain that you lure Sima Yi out to fight. You must not win; you are only to feign defeat. He will surely pursue you; then withdraw toward the place where the seven-star banner stands. If it is night, flee toward the seven lamps. You need only draw Sima Yi into Gourd Valley; I have my own plan to capture him.” Wei Yan received the plan and led his troops away. Kongming next summoned Gao Xiang and instructed him: “Group the wooden oxen and gliding horses in bands of twenty or thirty, or forty or fifty, load each with grain, and drive them back and forth along the mountain roads. If the Wei troops seize them, that will count as your achievement.” Gao Xiang accepted the plan and departed, driving the wooden oxen and gliding horses. Kongming redeployed every contingent from Mount Qi, claiming merely that they were being sent to farm the land. He ordered them: “If any other troops come to fight, you may only feign defeat. Only if Sima Yi comes in person are you to combine your strength, attack Weinan alone, and cut off his route of return.” When Kongming had completed all his dispositions, he personally led one army to encamp near Shangfang Valley.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He entered the camp and reported to Sima Yi: “The Shu troops have scattered to establish camps and are farming the land everywhere, intending to remain for a long campaign. Unless we destroy them now, once they have dwelt securely for long enough to put down deep and firm roots, they will be difficult to dislodge.” Sima Yi said, “This must be another of Kongming’s schemes.” The two replied, “If the Commander remains so suspicious and hesitant, when will the enemy ever be destroyed? We brothers will fight with all our strength in a battle to the death, and thus repay the nation’s favor.” Sima Yi said, “If that is so, you two may divide your forces and go out to battle.” He then ordered Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He each to lead five thousand troops, and they departed. Sima Yi sat awaiting their report.

p.src: Now Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He divided their troops between two routes. As they advanced, they suddenly saw Shu soldiers approaching with wooden oxen and gliding horses. Both charged upon them at once. The Shu troops fled in a great rout, and the Wei troops seized every wooden ox and gliding horse and sent them to Sima Yi’s camp. The next day, they captured more than a hundred men and horses, which they likewise sent to the main camp. Sima Yi interrogated the Shu soldiers brought before him to learn the true situation. The Shu soldiers told him, “Kongming reckoned only that the Commander would hold fast and refuse to come out, so he ordered all of us to scatter and farm the land in preparation for a long campaign. We never expected to be captured.” Sima Yi immediately released all the Shu soldiers and sent them back. Xiahou He asked, “Why not kill them?” Sima Yi replied, “They are merely common soldiers; killing them would serve no purpose. By releasing them to their own camp, we shall have them proclaim the generosity and benevolence of Wei’s commanders, thus weakening their comrades’ will to fight. This is the stratagem Lü Meng used to take Jingzhou.” He then issued an order that henceforth every captured Shu soldier was to be treated kindly and sent back, while officers and soldiers who distinguished themselves were to be richly rewarded. The commanders all received the order and departed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming ordered Gao Xiang to pretend to transport provisions, driving wooden oxen and gliding horses back and forth through Shangfang Valley. Xiahou Hui and the others repeatedly intercepted and attacked them. Within half a month, they won several battles in succession. Sima Yi rejoiced to see the Shu troops repeatedly defeated. One day, several dozen more Shu soldiers were captured. Sima Yi summoned them before his tent and asked, “Where is Kongming now?” They replied, “Chancellor Zhuge is not at Mount Qi. He has established camp ten li west of Shangfang Valley and is staying there. Provisions are now transported into Shangfang Valley and stored there every day.” After questioning them closely in every detail, Sima Yi released them. He then summoned his commanders and ordered them: “Kongming is no longer at Mount Qi but has encamped in Shangfang Valley. Tomorrow, all of you are to unite your strength and seize the main camp at Mount Qi. I shall personally lead troops to support you.” The commanders received their orders and each prepared for battle. Sima Shi asked, “Father, why do you instead intend to attack their rear?” Sima Yi replied, “Mount Qi is the foundation of the Shu army. When they see our forces attack it, every camp will surely rush to its aid. I shall then take Shangfang Valley and burn their provisions, leaving their head and tail unable to support each other; they are certain to suffer a crushing defeat.” Sima Shi bowed in admiration. Sima Yi immediately set his army in motion, ordering Zhang Hu and Yue Chen each to lead five thousand troops in support from the rear.

p.src: Seeing that Wei Yan was alone and had few troops, Sima Yi pursued him without misgiving. He ordered Sima Shi to take the left and Sima Zhao the right, while he himself held the center, and together they pressed the attack. Wei Yan led all five hundred of his soldiers in retreat into the valley. On reaching the valley mouth, Sima Yi first sent men inside to scout. They returned to report that there were no ambush troops in the valley and only thatched huts on the hills. Sima Yi said, “This must be where they store their provisions.” He therefore drove his entire force of men and horses into the valley. Sima Yi suddenly noticed that the thatched huts were covered with dry firewood, while Wei Yan had vanished from sight ahead. Growing suspicious, he said to his two sons, “What shall we do if troops cut off the valley mouth?” Before he had finished speaking, tremendous cries arose, and torches were hurled down from every part of the hills, setting the valley mouth ablaze and cutting off escape. The Wei troops had no road by which to flee. Fire arrows rained down from the hills, the mines erupted all at once, and the dry wood inside the huts caught fire with a deafening roar, sending flames soaring to the sky. Sima Yi was so terrified that he knew not what to do. Dismounting, he embraced his two sons and cried aloud, “All three of us, father and sons, shall die here!” As they wept, a violent gale suddenly arose and black clouds filled the sky. With a thunderclap, rain poured down in torrents. Every fire throughout the valley was extinguished. The mines failed to explode, and the incendiary devices proved useless. Sima Yi rejoiced and cried, “If we do not fight our way out now, what other moment are we waiting for?” He immediately led his troops in a desperate charge. Zhang Hu and Yue Chen also arrived with their respective forces to support him. Ma Dai had too few troops and dared not pursue. Sima Yi and his sons joined forces with Zhang Hu and Yue Chen, and together they returned to the main camp at Weinan. Unexpectedly, the camp and its palisades had already been seized by the Shu troops. Guo Huai and Sun Li were fighting the Shu troops on the pontoon bridge. When Sima Yi and the others arrived with their troops and attacked, the Shu troops withdrew. Sima Yi burned through the pontoon bridge and secured the northern bank.

u.src: Seeing that Wei Yan was alone and had few troops, Sima Yi pursued him without misgiving.
He ordered Sima Shi to take the left and Sima Zhao the right, while he himself held the center, and together they pressed the attack.
Wei Yan led all five hundred of his soldiers in retreat into the valley.
On reaching the valley mouth, Sima Yi first sent men inside to scout.
They returned to report that there were no ambush troops in the valley and only thatched huts on the hills.
Sima Yi said, “This must be where they store their provisions.”
He therefore drove his entire force of men and horses into the valley.
Sima Yi suddenly noticed that the thatched huts were covered with dry firewood, while Wei Yan had vanished from sight ahead.
Growing suspicious, he said to his two sons, “What shall we do if troops cut off the valley mouth?”
Before he had finished speaking, tremendous cries arose, and torches were hurled down from every part of the hills, setting the valley mouth ablaze and cutting off escape.
The Wei troops had no road by which to flee.
Fire arrows rained down from the hills, the mines erupted all at once, and the dry wood inside the huts caught fire with a deafening roar, sending flames soaring to the sky.
Sima Yi was so terrified that he knew not what to do. Dismounting, he embraced his two sons and cried aloud, “All three of us, father and sons, shall die here!”
As they wept, a violent gale suddenly arose and black clouds filled the sky.
With a thunderclap, rain poured down in torrents.
Every fire throughout the valley was extinguished.
The mines failed to explode, and the incendiary devices proved useless.
Sima Yi rejoiced and cried, “If we do not fight our way out now, what other moment are we waiting for?”
He immediately led his troops in a desperate charge.
Zhang Hu and Yue Chen also arrived with their respective forces to support him.
Ma Dai had too few troops and dared not pursue.
Sima Yi and his sons joined forces with Zhang Hu and Yue Chen, and together they returned to the main camp at Weinan.
Unexpectedly, the camp and its palisades had already been seized by the Shu troops.
Guo Huai and Sun Li were fighting the Shu troops on the pontoon bridge.
When Sima Yi and the others arrived with their troops and attacked, the Shu troops withdrew.
Sima Yi burned through the pontoon bridge and secured the northern bank.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Wei troops attacking the Shu encampment at Mount Qi heard that Sima Yi had suffered a crushing defeat and lost his camp south of the Wei River, throwing their army into confusion; when they hastily retreated, Shu troops charged them from every side. The Wei army was routed, eight or nine men in ten were wounded, and countless soldiers died; the survivors fled across to the north bank of the Wei River to save their lives. From the mountain, Kongming saw Wei Yan lure Sima Yi into the valley, and in an instant flames rose high. He was greatly delighted, believing that Sima Yi must surely die this time; but unexpectedly a great rain fell from heaven, and the fire would not catch. A scout reported that Sima Yi and his sons had all escaped. Kongming sighed, “Man proposes, but Heaven disposes. It cannot be forced!” A later poet lamented this in verse:

p.src: Now Sima Yi issued an order from his camp north of the Wei River: “The stockade south of the river has now been lost. Any commander who speaks again of giving battle shall be executed.” The commanders obeyed and held their ground without coming forth. Guo Huai entered and reported, “Recently Kongming has been leading troops out on reconnaissance. He must be choosing a place to make camp.” Sima Yi said, “If Kongming comes out through Wugong and advances eastward along the mountains, we shall all be in peril; but if he comes out south of the Wei River and halts in the west at Wuzhang Plains, there will be nothing to fear.” He sent men to investigate, and they returned to report that Kongming had indeed encamped at Wuzhang Plains. Sima Yi raised a hand to his brow and exclaimed, “This is due to the boundless good fortune of the Emperor of Great Wei!” He then ordered his commanders to hold firm and not come out, saying that if the enemy remained there long enough, troubles would arise among them of their own accord.

p.src: When Sima Yi had finished reading, he was furious inwardly; but he feigned a laugh and said, “Does Kongming take me for a woman?” He accepted the gifts at once and ordered that the messenger be treated with great courtesy. Sima Yi asked, “How are Kongming’s sleeping and eating, and how heavy is the burden of his duties?” The messenger replied, “The Chancellor rises early and retires late, and personally reviews every punishment of twenty strokes or more. As for food, he eats no more than a few sheng each day.” Turning to his commanders, Sima Yi said, “Kongming eats little and labors over many affairs. How can he last long?” The messenger took his leave and returned to Wuzhang Plains. On seeing Kongming, he gave a full account: “Sima Yi accepted the woman’s headdress and garments and read the letter, yet showed no anger. He asked only about Your Excellency’s sleeping and eating and the burden of your duties, and said nothing at all about military affairs. I answered him as I have told you, whereupon he said, ‘He eats little and has many affairs to attend to—how can he endure for long?’” Kongming sighed. “He understands me deeply!” Chief Clerk Yang Yong said, “I have often seen Your Excellency personally checking the registers and documents, and I have privately thought it unnecessary. There is a proper order to governing: superiors and subordinates must not encroach upon one another’s duties. Consider the management of a household: the male servants must be made to till the fields and the maids to oversee the cooking, so that no private task is neglected and every need is supplied. The master of the house may then remain calm and at ease, doing no more than sleeping soundly and taking his meals. But if he personally attends to everything, his body will grow weary and his mind exhausted, and in the end nothing will be accomplished. Is that because his wisdom is inferior to that of his maids and servants? No—it is because he has lost sight of the proper way to be master of a household. Thus the ancients called those who sat and discoursed upon the Way the Three Excellencies; those who rose and put it into practice they called scholar-officials. In former times, Bing Ji concerned himself with an ox panting for breath, yet did not inquire about the dead man lying across the road; and Chen Ping did not know the exact sums of money and grain, saying, ‘There are officials responsible for those matters.’ Now Your Excellency personally handles petty affairs and sweats at them all day long. How can this not exhaust you? Sima Yi’s words are indeed words of perfect truth.” Kongming wept and said, “It is not that I do not understand this. But the late Emperor entrusted his orphaned heir to me, so grave was his charge, and I fear only that others will not devote themselves as wholeheartedly as I do!” Everyone lowered his head and wept. From that time onward, Kongming himself felt his mind and spirits unsettled, and for this reason the commanders dared not advance.

Filled with indignation, they entered his tent and said, “We are all renowned commanders of a great realm. How can we endure such an insult from the men of Shu? If we rashly go forth now, we shall be defying our sovereign’s command.” The commanders remained indignant and dissatisfied. Sima Yi said, “Since you are determined to fight, wait until I obtain the Son of Heaven’s approval; then we shall join forces and confront the enemy. What say you?” The commanders agreed. p.src: After reading it, Cao Rui said to the assembled officials, “Sima Yi has held firm and refused to come forth. Why does he now submit a memorial asking to fight?” Xin Pi, Commandant of the Guards, said, “Sima Yi has never had any intention of fighting. He must have submitted this memorial only because Zhuge Liang humiliated him and his commanders grew indignant. He wishes to obtain another explicit command from Your Majesty, merely to restrain their ardor.” Cao Rui agreed and at once ordered Xin Pi to take the imperial credentials to the camp north of the Wei River and proclaim that no battle was to be fought. Sima Yi received the edict and entered the command tent, where Xin Pi proclaimed: “If anyone again dares speak of giving battle, he shall be judged guilty of defying the imperial command.” The commanders had no choice but to obey the edict. Sima Yi privately said to Xin Pi, “You truly understand my heart.” Thereupon word was spread throughout the army that the Emperor of Wei had sent Xin Pi with the imperial credentials to command Sima Yi not to give battle. The Shu commanders heard of this and reported it to Kongming. Kongming laughed and said, “This is Sima Yi’s method of pacifying his whole army.” Jiang Wei asked, “How does Your Excellency know this?” Kongming replied, “He never intended to fight; he asked for battle only to make a show of valor before his men. Have you not heard the saying, ‘When a general is in the field, there are commands from his sovereign that he need not accept’? What general would send a thousand li to request permission to fight? Because his officers were indignant, Sima Yi borrowed Cao Rui’s authority to keep them under control. And now he spreads this story abroad because he wishes to weaken the resolve of our army.”

p.src: While they were still discussing this, a sudden report came that Fei Yi had arrived, and Kongming had him brought in and questioned him. Fei Yi said, “When Cao Rui, Emperor of Wei, heard that Eastern Wu was advancing by three routes, he personally led a great army to Hefei and ordered Man Chong, Tian Yu, and Liu Shao to divide their forces into three columns to meet the enemy. By a stratagem, Man Chong burned all of Eastern Wu’s provisions and military equipment, while sickness spread among the Wu troops. Lu Xun sent a memorial to the King of Wu proposing that their forces coordinate an attack from front and rear, but unexpectedly the bearer of the memorial was captured on the way by Wei troops; thus the plan was exposed, and the Wu army returned without accomplishing anything.” When Kongming heard this news, he heaved a long sigh and suddenly collapsed unconscious to the ground; the commanders hurried to revive him, and only after a long while did he regain consciousness. Kongming sighed, “My mind is dazed and disordered, and my old illness has returned. I fear I shall not live!” That night, though ill, Kongming had himself helped out of his tent and gazed up at the heavens. Greatly alarmed, he returned inside and said to Jiang Wei, “My life will end within a day or two!” Jiang Wei asked, “Why does Your Excellency say this?” Kongming said, “Among the stars of the Three Terraces, I see the guest star shining with doubled brilliance, while the ruling star is dim and hidden, and the attendant stars arrayed beside it give only a faint light. With the heavens displaying such signs, my fate is plain to know!” Jiang Wei said, “Though the signs in the heavens are so, why does Your Excellency not employ a rite of prayer and expiation to reverse your fate?” Kongming replied, “I have long understood the rites of prayer and expiation, but I do not yet know what Heaven intends. Lead forty-nine armored soldiers here, each carrying a black banner and dressed in black, and have them form a ring outside my tent; I shall perform the rite within and pray to the Northern Dipper. If the chief lamp does not go out within seven days, my life may be extended by twelve years; but if the lamp is extinguished, I shall surely die. Do not allow any unauthorized person to enter. Whatever articles are needed shall be carried in only by two young attendants.” Jiang Wei received the order and went to make the preparations.

p.src: It was the Mid-Autumn Festival in the eighth month. That night, the Silver River shone brightly and pearly dew fell in glistening drops; the banners hung motionless, and not a sound came from the watchmen's gongs. Outside the tent, Jiang Wei led forty-nine men in standing guard. Within the tent, Kongming himself arranged incense, flowers, and sacrificial offerings. On the ground he set out seven large lamps, surrounded them with forty-nine smaller lamps, and placed within them a single lamp representing his own life. Kongming bowed and prayed: “I, Liang, was born into an age of turmoil and would gladly have grown old amid forests and streams; but having received the grace of Emperor Zhaolie, who visited me three times, and the grave charge of caring for his orphaned heir, I dared not fail to exhaust myself in faithful service and vowed to destroy the traitors to the realm. I did not foresee that my general's star would be about to fall and my allotted span to end. I have therefore reverently written this brief petition and report it to the vault of Heaven. I humbly beseech Heaven in its mercy to look down and heed my plea, graciously prolonging your servant's years, that I may repay my sovereign's favor above, save the lives of the people below, recover the old dominions, and perpetuate the sacrifices of Han forever. I dare not pray for this presumptuously; my feelings are truly desperate.” When he had finished his prayer, he prostrated himself inside the tent and waited for dawn. The next day he attended to affairs despite his illness, all the while coughing up blood without cease; by day he deliberated on military strategy, and by night he paced the Dipper's pattern in ritual observance.

p.src: Meanwhile, Sima Yi remained firmly on the defensive in his camp. One night, he suddenly looked up and observed the heavens, then said to Xiahou Ba with great delight: “I see that the general's star has strayed from its place. Kongming must be ill and will soon die. Take a thousand soldiers to Wuzhang Plains and scout the enemy. If the men of Shu fall into confusion and do not come out to engage you, Kongming is certainly stricken with illness. I shall then seize the opportunity to attack.” Xiahou Ba led his troops away. Kongming had now performed his rite of supplication inside the tent for six nights. Seeing the principal lamp still burning brightly, he was greatly heartened. When Jiang Wei entered the tent, he saw Kongming with hair unbound and sword in hand, pacing the pattern of the Dipper to hold the general's star in place.
